source.title: Exact Record Omission in Delta Attention: A Transport Criterion, Its Cost, and a Replay Certificate

page_placements.theme: Agents, context memory and tools resupply or retain forgotten information

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests inference-time memory edits and finds that suppressing direct answers can leave detectable information and a non-reference state. It also qualifies that result by access type and tests replay as a counter-method.
record.gate_note: This study concerns inference-time recurrent memory, not unlearning model weights. It tests attention masking, receipt corrections, prompt-forgetting instructions, and replay on recorded synthetic or other contexts. The fixed candidate-scoring probe uses known candidate values and probability access; the authors explicitly do not test arbitrary adaptive prompting, relearning, or generation-only attacks. The matched bf16/8-bit comparison is a precision control for receipt mismatch, not a test that quantization of unlearned weights restores knowledge.
record.test_reason: The study edits inference-time context memory (KDA recurrent state and MLA caches) of frozen models. It tests attention masking, receipt subtraction, prompt-forgetting and checkpoint replay on records supplied in the conversation. None of the claim's versions is tested: they concern unlearning knowledge stored in model weights (WMDP/RMU, Harry Potter, gradient-based methods) and attacks recovering it. Here no weights are changed, and nothing is learned in training and then removed. The paper frames this as analogous to unlearning and cites WMDP, Lynch et al. and Hu et al. only in related work. Its core finding, that answer suppression differs from removal, parallels version C but concerns a different kind of system and operation. It is recorded under fits_no_version. The 8-bit/bf16 comparison is a precision control on receipt mismatch, not quantization of unlearned weights.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Authors conclude that answer suppression does not establish removal: masking left candidate-detectable information, receipt transport fails exactly when later forcing is nonzero, and checkpoint replay matched the declared never-stored state. Replay does not cover earlier outputs, external copies or causally regenerated content. Authors note they did not test adaptive, generation-only or relearning attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The study edits inference-time recurrent state and attention entries, not model weights through gradient ascent, RMU, or the other named parameter-unlearning methods. It also tests checkpoint replay by recomputing the surviving recorded suffix.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on the edit (masking, receipt correction, or replay), suffix and corpus, and the access/measure used. Attention masking alone yielded AUC 0.740; masking plus transport yielded 0.519; replay yielded 0.500. Receipt residuals vary across selected layers and suffixes. Prompt forgetting is compared with a token-matched neutral instruction.

fits_no_version.finding: In inference-time recurrent memory (Kimi Linear 48B), attention masking removed all 40 exact direct answers. A three-query candidate-scoring attack still separated masked from never-stored contexts (AUC 0.740, 30% detection vs 7.5% FPR), and residual lift was 0.486 nats/token.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing direct answers to an in-context record does not remove its influence from recurrent/hybrid model memory; probability-access attacks detect it.

fits_no_version.finding: An instruction to forget an in-context record still returned the target in 33/40 contexts, with 100% detection and lift 3.121 nats/token.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-only forgetting instructions barely remove in-context information.

fits_no_version.finding: Subtracting a transported boundary receipt left nonzero native state residuals in Kimi, Qwen3.5 and three other families, because later updates create forcing. Receipt-corrected states still gave greedy target recovery in every sweep configuration. Matrix-only correction overshot on Mamba-2/RWKV-7 and left the lift nearly intact on Falcon-H1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subtracting a record's stored footprint from recurrent memory does not reach the never-stored state when later processing depended on it.

fits_no_version.finding: Checkpoint replay matched the never-stored state and logits exactly in 80/80 contexts. The fixed attack performed at the null level and all 120 retained answers were preserved.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Exact recomputation from a pre-record checkpoint yields verifiable removal of in-context records under the audited state and fixed attack.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking plus transport reduced residual signal to AUC 0.519 and detection to the null rate, but with small positive lift.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combining attention masking with recurrent correction nearly but not exactly removes detectable in-context information.

record.problems: The main prospective cohort has 40 evaluation and 40 calibration contexts, all synthetic and on one model. The attack assumes known candidate values and probability-score access and uses only three fixed queries. Its measured false-positive-rate interval is broad. Authors state that adaptive attacks, generation-only attacks, relearning, broader task utility, and causal regeneration are not tested. Some utility checks use a small synthetic passage bank.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed suffix-cut, layer, corpus, and sampled-generation tables are not expanded into separate rows; the main aggregate findings on receipt residuals, target recovery, and masking KL are recorded in R19 and R21–R23. Resource/storage measurements and record-amendment results were omitted because they do not measure the claim versions’ recovery attacks. The precision comparison is recorded only as a receipt-mismatch control (R30–R31), not as a quantization-recovery result.

untested.parts: No weight-unlearning method, no forget-set knowledge accuracy versus chance, no general-ability benchmark. Edits act on in-context memory of frozen models.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of unlearned weights. State-residual analysis concerns context memory.
No quantization of unlearned weights; bf16/8-bit is a precision control.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery attack on unlearned knowledge.
Checkpoint replay is context recomputation, not a robust weight-unlearning method.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to nonexistent version IDs (V1/V3/V6). On review, no row bears on any version, because the system and operation differ: in-context memory deletion in frozen models versus unlearning trained knowledge from weights. All the reader's labels are therefore dropped. The study is conceptually close to version C's 'blocks access rather than deletes' finding, so its results are logged under fits_no_version for a possible inference-time-memory claim. R05, R17 and R20 are controls rather than result rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests direct-answer suppression, retained-record utility, and a fixed candidate-scoring attack for inference-time edits, not gradient-ascent, RMU, or other parameter unlearning methods.
No fine-tuning or relearning set is used.
No activation-direction ablation is tested. The study analyzes recurrent-state differences and attention masking, rather than ablating an activation direction.
The precision comparison does not quantize unlearned weights to test recovery; it measures receipt-transport mismatch in matched bf16 and 8-bit models.

The study does not test rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information as recovery attacks. Its fixed candidate-scoring probe requires probability access; prompt-forgetting is an edit condition, not a prompt-only recovery attack.
Replay is tested against the specified state/logit audits and fixed scoring probe, not against fine-tuning, adaptive prompting, generation-only attacks, or every attack named in the claim.

relation.reason: Weight-space unlearning appears only in related work and the index terms. The paper's 'answer suppression is not removal' theme parallels the claim but is studied for context memory. The reader's tests/T5 call does not fit.

tranche.reason: The study edits the inference-time context memory (KDA state, MLA caches) of frozen models. Model weights remain fixed, so none of versions A-F, which concern unlearned weights, is tested.

source_check.notes: All three rows match Table IV and Table VI (also Table V for lift). The rows cover in-context prompt forgetting on 8-bit Kimi Linear with frozen weights, not weight unlearning, so they are comparators only. Detection assumes known candidate values and log-probability access.

statements.correction: Prompt forgetting on 8-bit Kimi Linear (40 prospective synthetic contexts): 33/40 exact target answers on the direct greedy query, 100% detection by the fixed three-query candidate-scoring attack, lift 3.121 nats/token (record present 40/40, lift 3.240). This is inference-time context memory with frozen weights, not weight unlearning.
